concerning Jeroboam son of Nebat and the sins he committed and caused Israel to commit, greatly provoking the Lord, the God of Israel, to anger.
The rest of Nadab's deeds and everything he did are recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.
There was war between Baasha and Asa king of Judah throughout their lives.
In the third year of King Asa of Judah, Baasha son of Ahijah became king over all Israel in Tirzah, and he reigned for twenty-four years.
He did what was evil in the Lord's sight and followed the ways of Jeroboam son of Nebat and the sins he had caused Israel to commit.
The word of the Lord came to Jehu son of Hanani concerning Baasha, saying:

This is what the Lord says: “Because I raised you from the dust and made you ruler over my people Israel, but you followed the ways of Jeroboam and caused my people Israel to sin, provoking me to anger by the work of their hands,
look, I will sweep away Baasha and his house. I will make his house like the house of Jeroboam son of Nebat.”
The dogs will eat anyone belonging to Baasha who dies in the city, and the birds of the sky will eat anyone belonging to him who dies in the open country.”
The rest of Baasha's deeds, everything he did, and all his mighty achievements are recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.
Baasha lay down with his ancestors and was buried in Tirzah. His son Elah became king after him.

The word of the Lord also came through the prophet Jehu son of Hanan against Baasha and his entire house, because of all the evil he had done in the Lord's sight, provoking him to anger by the work of his hands and becoming like the house of Jeroboam, and because he had killed him.
In the twenty-sixth year of King Asa of Judah, Elah son of Baasha became king over Israel in Tirzah, and he reigned for two years.
His servant Zimri, commander of half the chariots, rebelled against him while he was in Tirzah, drinking aged wine in the house of [?] that he had built in Tirzah.
Zimri came in, struck him down, and killed him in the twenty-seventh year of King Asa of Judah, and succeeded him as king.
When he became king and sat on his throne, he struck down the entire house of Baasha. He left him no one who urinated against a wall, and killed all his relatives and friends.
Zimri destroyed the entire house of Baasha according to the word of the Lord that he had spoken against Baasha through Jehu the prophet.
This was because of all the sins of Baasha and the sins of his son Elah, which they committed and caused Israel to commit, provoking the Lord, the God of Israel, to anger with their idols.
The rest of Elah's deeds and everything he did are recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.
In the twenty-seventh year of King Asa of Judah, Zimri reigned for seven days in Tirzah. The people were encamped against Gath of the Philistines.
The people in the camp heard it being said, “Zimri has rebelled and has also killed the king.” That day, in the camp, all Israel made Omri, the army commander, king over Israel.
Omri went up from Gath, with all Israel accompanying him, and they encamped against Tirzah.
When Zimri saw that Tirzah had been captured, he went into the inner chamber of the royal palace. They set the royal palace on fire over him, and he died.
This was because of the sins he had committed, doing evil before the Lord by following the ways of Jeroboam son of Nebat and the sins by which he had led Israel into sin.
The rest of Zimri’s deeds and the rebellion he carried out are recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.
Then the people of Israel split into factions. Half the people followed Tibni son of Ginath to make him king, and half followed Omri.
The people who followed Omri proved stronger than the people who followed Tibni. Tibni died, and Omri became king.
In the thirty-first year of Asa king of Judah, Omri became king over Israel for twelve years. He reigned in Tirzah for six years.
He bought the hill of Samaria from Shemer for a talent of silver and built on the hill. He named the town he built Samaria, after Shemer, the owner of the hill.
Omri did what was evil in the sight of the Lord and acted more wickedly than all the kings who were before him.
He followed all the ways of Jeroboam son of Nebat and the sins by which he had led Israel into sin, provoking the Lord, the God of Israel, to anger with their idols.
The rest of Omri’s deeds, everything he did, and all his mighty acts are recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.
Omri rested with his ancestors and was buried in Samaria. His son Ahab became king after him.
Ahab son of Omri became king over Israel in the thirty-eighth year of Asa king of Judah. Ahab son of Omri reigned over Israel in Samaria for twenty-two years.
Ahab son of Omri did more evil in the sight of the Lord than all who were before him.

As though following the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat were a trivial matter in his eyes, he went and married Jezebel, daughter of Ethbaal king of the Sidonians. He went and served Baal and bowed down to him.
He set up an altar for Baal in the temple of Baal that he built in Samaria.
Ahab served idols, and Ahab went further in serving them and provoking the Lord, the God of Israel, to anger than all the kings of Israel who had been before him.

In his days Ahab built Jericho, the house of the curse. He completed it at the cost of Abiram his firstborn, and set up its gates at the cost of Segub his youngest, according to the word of the Lord that he had spoken through Joshua son of Nun.

Elijah, who was from Tishbe, one of the settlers of Gilead, said to King Ahab, “As the Lord, the God of Israel, lives, before whom I stand, there will be neither dew nor rain during these years except when I say so.”
The word of the Lord came to him and said to him:
“Leave here, turn eastward, and hide by the brook Cherith, which is east of the Jordan.
You will drink from the brook, and I have commanded the ravens to feed you there.”
He went and did according to the word of the Lord. He went and stayed by the brook Cherith, which is east of the Jordan.
The ravens brought him bread and meat in the morning and bread and meat in the evening, and he drank water from the brook.
After some days the streams dried up, because no rain had fallen on the land.
The word of the Lord came to him, saying:
“Get up, go to Zarephath in Sidon, and stay there. I have commanded a widow there to feed you.”
He got up and went to Zarephath. He entered the town gate and saw a widow there gathering wood. He called to her and said, “Bring me a little water in a vessel so that I may drink.”
As she went to bring it to him, he called to her and said, “Bring me a piece of bread in your hand.”

She said, “As the Lord your God lives, I have nothing except a handful of flour in a jar and a little oil in a horn. Here I am gathering two sticks so that I can go and prepare something for myself and my son. We will eat it and die.”
Elijah said to her, “Do not be afraid. Go and do as you have said. Only make a small cake first and bring it out to me. Afterward, make something for yourself and your son.”
“For this is what the Lord, the God of Israel, says: ‘The jar of flour will not run out, and the horn of oil will not fail, until the day the Lord sends rain upon the earth.’”
She went and did as Elijah had said, and she, he, and the members of his household ate during those days.
The jar of flour did not run out, and the horn of oil did not fail, according to the word of the Lord that he had spoken through Elijah.
After these things, the son of the woman who owned the house became ill. His illness became so severe that no breath remained in him.
She said to Elijah, “What do you have against me, prophet of God? Have you come to me to bring my sins to remembrance and to kill my son?”
Elijah said to her, “Give me your son.” He took him from her lap, carried him up to the upstairs room where he was staying, and laid him on his bed.
He called out to the Lord and said, “Lord God, have you brought disaster even on this widow with whom I am staying, by killing her son?”
He stretched himself over the boy three times and called out to the Lord, saying, “Lord my God, let this boy’s soul return into him.”
The LORD heard Elijah’s voice, and the boy’s soul returned to him, and he came to life.
Elijah took the boy, brought him down from the upstairs room into the house, and gave him to his mother. Elijah said to her, “Look, your son is alive!”
She said, “Now I know that you are a prophet of God, and that the word of the LORD in your mouth is true.”
After many days, in the third year, the word of the Lord came to Elijah, saying, “Go and present yourself to Ahab, and I will send rain upon the earth.”
Elijah went to present himself to Ahab. The famine was severe in Samaria.
Ahab summoned Obadiah, who was in charge of his household. Obadiah feared the LORD greatly.
When Jezebel was killing the prophets of God, Obadiah took a hundred prophets and hid them in a cave in groups of fifty, and supplied them with bread and water.

Ahab said to Obadiah, “Go through the land to all the springs of water and all the streams. Perhaps we will find grass and keep the horses and mules alive, so that we do not lose any of the livestock.”
They divided the territory between them to travel through it. Ahab went alone along one route, and Obadiah went alone along another route.
While Obadiah was on the road, Elijah met him. Obadiah recognized him, fell facedown, and said to him, “Is it you, my lord Elijah?”
He said to him, “It is I.” Then he said to him, “Go, tell your master, ‘Elijah is here.’”
Obadiah said, “What sin have I committed, that you are handing your servant over to Ahab to have me killed?”

“As the LORD your God lives, there is no nation or kingdom where my master has not sent someone to look for you. When they said, ‘He is not here,’ he made the kingdoms and nations swear that they had not found you.
“And now you tell me, ‘Go, tell your master, “Elijah is here.”’”

When I leave you, the Spirit of the LORD will carry you away and take you somewhere I do not know. Then I will go to tell Ahab, but he will not find you, and he will kill me. Yet your servant has feared the LORD from his youth.

Was my lord not told what I did when Jezebel killed the prophets of God? I took a hundred men from among the prophets of the LORD and hid them in a cave, fifty men at a time, and supplied them with bread and water.”
“And now you tell me, ‘Go, tell your master, “Elijah is here,”’ and he will kill me!”
Elijah said, “As the LORD Almighty lives, whom I serve, I will surely present myself to him today.”
Obadiah went to meet Ahab and told him, and Ahab came to meet Elijah.
When Ahab saw Elijah, he said to him, “Is it you, the one who troubles Israel?”
Elijah said to him, “I have not brought trouble on Israel. Rather, you and your father’s household have, because you have abandoned the LORD’s commandments and followed Baal.
Now send and gather all Israel to me at Mount Carmel, along with the four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal and the four hundred and fifty prophets of the idols who eat at Jezebel’s table.”
Ahab sent word throughout all the Israelites and gathered the men at Mount Carmel.
Elijah approached all the people and said, “How long will you remain divided between two sides? If the LORD is God, follow him; but if Baal is, follow him.” The people gave him no answer.
Elijah said, “I alone remain as a prophet of the LORD, but the prophets of Baal number four hundred and fifty men.

Let them give us two bulls. Let them choose one bull for themselves, cut it into pieces, and lay it on the wood, but put no fire under it. I will prepare the other bull, cut it into pieces, and lay it on the wood, but I will put no fire under it.
Call on the names of your gods, and I will call on the name of the LORD my God. The god who answers with fire is God.” All the people answered, “You have spoken well.”
Elijah said to the prophets of Baal, “Choose one bull for yourselves and prepare it first, because you are many.”

They took the bull that had been given to them and prepared it. They called on the name of Baal from morning until noon, saying, “Baal, answer us!” But there was no voice and no one answered. They beat themselves against the altar they had made.

At noon Elijah mocked them and said, “Call out loudly, for he is a god! Perhaps he is deep in thought, or perhaps he is attending to some business, or perhaps he is on a journey. Or perhaps he is asleep and must be awakened.”
They called out loudly and cut themselves with swords and spears, as was their custom, until their blood poured over them.

After noon had passed, they continued prophesying until the time when the offering was presented. But there was no voice, no one answered, and no one paid attention. Elijah said to the prophets of the idols, “Move aside now, so that I too may prepare whole burnt offerings.” They moved aside and went away.
Elijah said to all the people, “Come near me.” All the people came near him, and he repaired the altar of the LORD that had been torn down.
Elijah took twelve stones, according to the number of the tribes of the sons of Jacob, to whom the word of the LORD had come, saying, “Your name shall be Israel.”
With the stones he built an altar in the name of the LORD. He made a trench around the altar large enough to hold two seahs of seed.
He arranged the wood, cut the bull into pieces, and laid it on top of the wood.

He said, “Fill four jars with water and pour it over the burnt offering and the wood.” Then he said, “Do it a second time,” and they did it a second time. He said, “Do it a third time,” and they did it a third time.
The water ran around the altar, and they also filled the trench with water.

At the time when the offering was presented, Elijah the prophet approached and said, “LORD, God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, let it be known today that you are God in Israel, that I am your servant, and that I have done all these things at your command.
Answer me, LORD, answer me, so that all these people may know that you, LORD, are God, and that you have turned their hearts back.”
The LORD’s fire fell and consumed the burnt offering, the wood, the stones, and the dust, and licked up the water in the trench.
All the people saw it, fell on their faces, and said, “The LORD is God! The LORD is God!”
Elijah said to them, “Seize the prophets of Baal! Do not let a single one of them escape!” They seized them, and Elijah brought them down to the Kishon stream and slaughtered them there.
Elijah said to Ahab, “Go up, eat and drink, for there is the sound of a downpour.”
Ahab went up to eat and drink. Elijah went up to the top of Carmel, bent down to the ground, and put his face between his knees.
He said to his disciple, “Go up and look toward the sea.” He went up, looked, and said, “There is nothing.” He told him, “Go back seven times.”

On the seventh time he said, “I looked, and there is a small cloud like the palm of a hand rising from the sea.” He said to him, “Go up and tell Ahab, ‘Get into your chariot and go down before the rain stops you.’”
While he was turning this way and that, the sky became covered with clouds and wind, and there was heavy rain. Ahab got into his chariot and went to Jezreel.
The hand of the Lord was upon Elijah. He fastened his belt around his waist and ran ahead of Ahab until he entered Jezreel.
Ahab told Jezebel everything Elijah had done, and how he had killed all the prophets of Baal and of [?] with the sword.
Jezebel sent a message to Elijah through a messenger, saying, “May the gods do this to me and more besides if, by this time tomorrow, I do not make your life like the life of one of them.”
Elijah was afraid and got up and went away to save his life. He came to Beersheba in Judah and left his disciple there.

He went a day’s journey into the wilderness and sat beneath a terebinth tree. He asked that he might die and said, “I have had enough now, Lord. Take my life from me, for I am no better than my ancestors.”
He lay down and fell sound asleep beneath the terebinth tree. Then an angel came up to him and said to him, “Get up and eat.”
He turned and saw at his head [?] bread baked on hot stones and a jar of water. He ate and drank, then lay down again.
The angel of the Lord returned a second time, came near him, and said, “Get up, eat and drink, for the journey is too much for you.”
He got up, ate and drank, and went on the strength of that food for forty days and forty nights, as far as Horeb, the mountain of God.
He entered a cave there and spent the night there. The word of the Lord came to him, saying, “What are you doing here, Elijah?”

He said, “I have been deeply zealous for the Lord, the mighty God, because the Israelites have abandoned your covenant, torn down your altars, and killed your prophets with the sword. I alone am left, and now they are seeking to take my life.”

He said to him, “Go out and stand on the mountain before the Lord.” And the Lord made a great and powerful wind that split mountains and shattered rocks before the Lord, but the Lord was not in the wind. After the wind came an earthquake, but the Lord was not in the earthquake.
After the earthquake came fire, but the Lord was not in the fire. After the fire came the sound of gentle speech.
When Elijah heard it, he wrapped his face in his cloak, went out, and stood at the entrance of the cave. A voice came to him and said, “What are you doing here, Elijah?”

He said, “I have been deeply zealous for the Lord, the mighty God, because the Israelites have abandoned your covenant, torn down your altars, and killed your prophets with the sword. I alone am left, and now they are seeking to take my life.”
The Lord said to him, “Go back on your way to the wilderness of Damascus, and go and anoint Hazael to reign over Edom.
And anoint Jehu son of Nimshi to reign over Israel, and Elisha son of Shaphat, from Abel-meholah, to be prophet in your place.
Whoever escapes the sword of Hazael, Jehu will kill; and whoever escapes the sword of Jehu, Elisha will kill.
I will leave seven thousand in Israel—all the knees that have not bowed to Baal and every mouth that has not kissed him.”
He went from there and found Elisha son of Shaphat driving a team of oxen. There were twelve teams before him, and he was with one of the twelve. Elijah passed by him and threw his cloak over him.
He left the team of oxen, went after Elijah, and said to him, “Let me go and kiss my father and mother, and then I will follow you.” He said to him, “Go back. What have I done to you?”

He turned back from following him, took the team of oxen, and slaughtered them. He cooked the meat using the oxen’s equipment, gave it to the people, and they ate. Then he got up, followed Elijah the prophet, and served him.
Ben-hadad king of Edom gathered his entire army, along with the thirty-two kings who were with him, horses, and chariots. He went up, laid siege to Samaria, and fought against it.
He sent messengers to Ahab king of Israel.
He said to him, “This is what Ben-hadad says: ‘Your silver and gold are mine, and your beautiful wives and children are mine.’”
The king of Israel answered, “As you say, my lord the king. I am yours, and so is everything I have.”
The messengers returned and said, “This is what Ben-hadad says: ‘I sent you word before that you must give me your silver and gold, your wives and children.
Tomorrow at this time I will send my servants to you. They will search your houses and your servants’ houses, and whatever their eyes desire they will take in their hands and bring away.’”

The king of Israel summoned all the elders of the land and said to them, “Understand and see that this man is seeking trouble. He sent to me for my wives and children, my silver and gold, and I did not withhold them from him.”
All the elders and all the people said to him, “Do not listen to him or agree to his demands.”

He said to Ben-hadad’s messengers, “Tell my lord the king: ‘I will do everything you first sent word to your servant to do, but I cannot do this thing.’” The messengers went and brought the answer back to him.
Ben-hadad sent word to him, saying, “May the gods do this to me and more besides if the dust of Samaria is enough to give each of the people with me a handful!”
The king of Israel answered, “Tell him, ‘Let the one who straps on his armor not be regarded as the one who takes it off.’”
When he heard this message, he and the kings were drinking in the shelters. He said to his servants, “Lay siege to the city!”

Then a prophet approached Ahab king of Israel and said to him, “This is what the Lord says: ‘Do you see this whole great army? Look, I am handing it over to you today, and you will know that I am the Lord.’”
Ahab said, “Through whom?” He answered him, “Through the young men and the officials of the city.” He asked him, “Who should begin the battle?” He answered him, “You.”
He counted the young men and the officials of the city, and they numbered 232. After them he counted all the people, all the Israelites: seven thousand.
They went out at noon, while Ben-hadad was drinking aged wine in the shelters with the thirty-two kings who had come to help him.
The young men and the officials of the city went out first. Ben-hadad sent men out, and they reported to him, saying, “Look, men have come out of Samaria.”
He said, “If they have come out for peace, capture them alive; and if they have come out for battle, capture them alive.”
These went out of the city: the young men and the officials of the province, with the army behind them.
Each man killed his opponent, and Edom fled. Israel pursued them, but Ben-hadad king of Edom escaped with chariots and horsemen.
The king of Israel went out and destroyed the horses and chariots, and inflicted a very great defeat on Edom.

Then the prophet of God approached Ahab king of Israel and said to him, “Go, strengthen yourself, and consider carefully what you must do, because at the turn of the year the king of Edom will come up against you.”
The servants of the king of Edom said to him, “Their God is a god of the mountains. That is why they defeated us. But let us fight them on the plain, and we will surely defeat them.”
Do this: remove each of the kings from his position and appoint commanders in their place.
“Muster an army equal to the army you lost, horse for horse and chariot for chariot. Let us fight them on the plain, and we will surely prove stronger than they are.” He listened to them and did so.
At the turn of the year, Ben-hadad mustered Edom and went up to Aphek to fight Israel.
The Israelites were counted and drawn up in formation. They stood facing them like two flocks of young goats, while the Edomites filled the land.

The prophet of God approached Ahab king of Israel and said to him, “This is what the Lord says: ‘Because the Edomites have said, “The Lord is a god of the mountains and not a god of the valleys,” I will hand this whole great army over to you, and you will know that I am the Lord.’”
They camped opposite one another for seven days. On the seventh day they joined battle, and the Israelites killed a hundred thousand Edomite foot soldiers in a single day.
Those who remained fled to the city of Aphek, and the wall fell on twenty-seven thousand of the survivors. Ben-hadad fled and entered the city, going into an inner room.

His servants approached him and said, “Look, we have heard that the kings of Israel are kind kings. Let us tie sackcloth around our heads and ropes around our waists and go out to the king of Israel. Perhaps he will spare our lives.”

They tied sackcloth around their heads and ropes around their waists and came to the king of Israel. They said to him, “Your servant Ben-hadad says, ‘Spare my life.’” He said, “Is he still alive? He is my brother.”

Ben-hadad was a man who practiced divination. The men stirred, hurried, and secured his release from him, saying, “Your brother Ben-hadad!” He said, “Go, bring him.” Ben-hadad came out to him, and he seated him beside himself in the chariot.

He said to him, “I will return to you the towns my father took from your father, and I will establish a marketplace for you in Damascus, as my father did in Samaria.” “And I will send you away under a treaty.” He made a treaty with him and sent him away.
One of the members of the prophetic community said to his companion at the Lord’s command, “Strike me.” But the man was unwilling to strike him.
He said to him, “Because you have not obeyed the Lord your God, as soon as you leave me, a lion will kill you.” He left him, and a lion found him and killed him.
He found another man and said to him, “Strike me.” That man struck him and wounded him.
The prophet went and stood beside the road before the king, covering his face with ashes.

As the king passed by, he cried out before the king and said, “Your servant went out into the battle, and a man turned aside and brought a man to me. He said to me, ‘Guard this man. If he escapes, your life will be given for his life, or you must pay a talent of silver.’”
“While your servant was turning this way and that, the man disappeared.” The king of Israel said to him, “That is your sentence; you have decided it yourself.”
He hurried and removed the ashes from his face, and the king of Israel recognized that he was one of the prophets.
And he said to him, “This is what the Lord says: Because you let the man condemned to destruction go [?], your life will be taken in place of his life, and your people in place of his people.”
The king of Israel went home, distressed and angry, and entered Samaria.
After these things, Naboth the Jezreelite had a vineyard in Jezreel beside the palace of Ahab king of Samaria.

Ahab said to Naboth, “Give me your vineyard so that I can make it a vegetable garden, because it is close beside my house. I will give you a better vineyard in exchange for it, or, if you prefer, I will give you its value in silver.”
Naboth said to Ahab, “The Lord forbid that I should give you my ancestors’ inheritance!”

Ahab went home distressed and angry because of what Naboth the Jezreelite had told him: “I will not give you my ancestors’ inheritance.” He lay down on his bed, turned his face away, and would not eat.
His wife Jezebel came to him and said, “Why are you so distressed that you do not want to eat?”

He said to her, “Because I said to Naboth the Jezreelite, ‘Give me your vineyard for silver, or, if you wish, I will give you a better vineyard in exchange for it.’ But he told me, ‘I will not give you my vineyard.’”
His wife Jezebel said to him, “Are you fit to be king over Israel? Get up, eat, and cheer up. I will give you the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite.”
She wrote a letter in Ahab’s name, sealed it with his signet ring, and sent the letter to the elders and nobles who lived in the town with Naboth.
She wrote in the letter, “Proclaim a fast and seat Naboth at the head of the people.
“Bring two wicked men and seat them opposite him. Have them testify against him and say, ‘Naboth cursed God and the king.’ Then take him out and stone him to death.”
The men of his town, the elders and nobles who lived in the town with Naboth, did as Jezebel had instructed them, as it was written in the letter she had sent them.
They proclaimed a fast and seated Naboth at the head of the people.

They brought two wicked men and seated them opposite him. Those men testified against Naboth, saying, “Naboth cursed God and the king.” They took him outside the town and stoned him with stones, and he died.
They sent word to Jezebel that Naboth had been stoned and had died.

When Jezebel heard that Naboth had died, she said to Ahab, “Get up and take possession of the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite, who refused to sell it to you for silver. Naboth is dead; he is no longer alive.”
When Ahab heard that Naboth had died, he got up to go down to the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite to take possession of it.
The word of the LORD came to Elijah from Tishbe, saying:
“Get up and go down to meet Ahab king of Israel, who is in Samaria. Look, he is in the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite, where he has gone down to take possession of it.”

“Say to him, ‘This is what the Lord says: Look, you have murdered, and now you have taken possession! This is what the Lord says: In the place where the dogs licked Naboth’s blood, the dogs will lick your blood too—your own blood.’”
Ahab said to Elijah, “Have you found me, my enemy?” He said to him, “I have found you, because you have acted arrogantly by doing evil before the Lord.
“Look, I am bringing disaster upon you. I will sweep away your descendants and destroy every male belonging to Ahab, bound or free in Israel.
“I will make your house like the house of Jeroboam son of Nebat and like the house of Baasha son of Ahijah, because you have provoked me to anger and caused Israel to sin.”
The LORD also said concerning Jezebel, ‘Dogs will eat Jezebel on the estate at Jezreel.’
Anyone belonging to Ahab who dies in the city, dogs will eat; and anyone belonging to him who dies in the open country, the birds of the sky will eat.”
Indeed, there was no one like Ahab, who set his mind on doing evil before the LORD, urged on by his wife Jezebel.
He defiled himself greatly and followed idols, just as the Amorites had done, whom the Lord destroyed before the Israelites.
When Ahab heard this message, he tore his clothes, put sackcloth over his body, fasted, lay down in sackcloth, and went about barefoot.
The word of the LORD came to Elijah from Tishbe, saying:

“Have you seen how Ahab has humbled himself before me? Because he has humbled himself before me, I will not bring the disaster during his lifetime. During his son’s lifetime I will bring the disaster upon his house.”
They remained for three years without war between Edom and Israel.
In the third year, Jehoshaphat king of Judah went down to Ahab king of Israel.
The king of Israel said to his servants, “You know that Ramoth-gilead belongs to us. How long will we remain inactive instead of taking it from the king of Edom?”
He said to Jehoshaphat, “Will you go with me to battle at Ramoth-gilead?” Jehoshaphat said, “I will go. I am as you are, my people are as your people, and my horses are as your horses.”
Jehoshaphat said to the king of Israel, “Please inquire today for the word of the LORD.”

The king of Israel gathered the prophets, about four hundred men, and said to them, “Should I go to battle at Ramoth-gilead, or should I refrain?” They said to him, “Go up! The Lord will deliver them into your hands, O king.”
Jehoshaphat said, “Is there no prophet of God here whom we can consult?”

The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, “There is still one man through whom we can inquire for the Lord’s word, but I hate him, because he never prophesies good about me, only disaster. His name is Micaiah son of Imlah.” Jehoshaphat said, “The king should not say that.”
The king of Israel called an official and said to him, “Quickly bring Micaiah son of Imlah.”
The king of Israel and Jehoshaphat king of Judah were sitting, each on his throne, wearing robes, [?], at the entrance to the gate of Samaria. All the prophets were prophesying before them.
Zedekiah son of Chenaanah made himself iron horns and said, “This is what the Lord says: With these you will gore the Edomites until you destroy them.”
All the prophets were prophesying the same thing, saying, “Go up to Ramoth-gilead, and you will be victorious. The Lord will hand them over to you, O king.”

The messenger who went to summon Micaiah said to him, “Look, the false prophets have unanimously spoken favorably about the king. Let your word be like the word of one of them, and speak favorably too.”
Micaiah said, “As the Lord lives, I will say only what the Lord tells me.”

He came to the king, and the king said to him, “Micaiah, shall we go to Ramoth-gilead for battle, or shall we stay here?” He said to him, “Go up and be victorious, and the Lord will hand them over to you, O king.”
The king said to him, “How many times must I make you swear to tell me nothing but the truth in the Lord’s name?”
Micaiah said, “I saw Israel scattered over the mountains like sheep without a shepherd. And the Lord said, ‘These people have no master. Let each return home in peace.’”
The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, “Did I not tell you that he prophesies nothing good about me, but only evil?”
Micaiah said, “Therefore, hear the word of the Lord: I saw the Lord sitting on his throne, with the whole army of heaven standing above him, on his right and on his left.”
The Lord said, “Who will entice Ahab to go up and fall at Ramoth-gilead?” One said one thing, and another said something else.
A spirit came forward, stood before the Lord, and said, “I will entice him.” The Lord said to him, “How?”
He said, “I will go out and become a lying spirit in the mouths of all his prophets.” He said to him, “You will entice him, and you will succeed. Go out and do so.”
“Now look, the Lord has put a lying spirit in the mouths of all these prophets of yours, and the Lord has spoken disaster against you.”
Zedekiah son of Chenaanah approached, struck Micaiah on the cheek, and said to him, “Which way did the Spirit of the Lord pass from me to speak through you?”
Micaiah said to him, “You will see on the day when you go into an inner room to hide.”
The king of Israel said, “Take Micaiah away and hand him over to Amon, the governor of the city, and to Joash, the king’s son.”
“And say, ‘This is what the king says: Put this man in prison, and give him only enough bread and water to keep him alive until I return safely.’”
Micaiah said, “If you do return safely, the Lord has not spoken through me.” And he said, “Listen, all you peoples!”
The king of Israel and Jehoshaphat king of Judah went up to Ramoth-gilead.
The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, “I will disguise myself and enter the battle, but you wear your own robes.” So the king of Israel disguised himself and entered the battle.
The king of Edom commanded his thirty-two chariot commanders, saying, “Do not fight anyone, small or great, except the king of Israel alone.”
When the chariot commanders saw Jehoshaphat, they thought he was the king of Israel. They turned toward him to fight him, and Jehoshaphat cried out.
When the chariot commanders saw that he was not the king of Israel, they turned away from him.

A certain man shot his bow straight ahead without knowing whom he would hit, and struck the king of Israel at a joint in his armor. The king said to his charioteer, “Turn around and take me out of the army, because the pains of death have come upon me.”
The battle grew fierce that day, and the king remained standing in his chariot facing Edom. He died in the evening, and the blood from his wound flowed into the bottom of his chariot.
At sunset a herald called out in the camp, saying, “Go, each man to his own city and each to his own land!”
The king died and was brought to Samaria, and they buried the king in Samaria.
They washed the chariot at the pool of Samaria, and they washed his armor. The dogs licked up his blood, according to the word the Lord had spoken.
The rest of Ahab’s deeds, everything he did, the ivory house he built, and all the cities he built are recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.
Ahab rested with his ancestors, and his son Ahaziah became king after him.
Jehoshaphat son of Asa became king over Judah in the fourth year of Ahab king of Israel.
Jehoshaphat was thirty-five years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem for twenty-five years. His mother’s name was Arubah daughter of Shilhi.
He followed all the ways of his father Asa and did not turn aside from them. He did what was right in the sight of the Lord.
However, he did not remove the high places, and the people continued to offer sacrifices and burn incense at the high places.
Jehoshaphat made peace with the kings of Israel.
The rest of Jehoshaphat’s deeds, all the mighty acts he performed, and the battles he fought are recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah.
He removed from the land the rest of the prostitution that had remained in the days of his father Asa.
There was no reigning king in Edom.
Jehoshaphat built ships for Tarshish to go to Ophir for gold, but they did not go, because the ships were wrecked at Ezion-geber.
Then Ahaziah son of Ahab said to Jehoshaphat, “Let my servants go with your servants in the ships.” But Jehoshaphat was unwilling.
Jehoshaphat rested with his ancestors and was buried with his ancestors in the city of David his ancestor. His son Jehoram became king in his place.
Ahaziah son of Ahab became king over Israel in Samaria in the seventeenth year of Jehoshaphat king of Judah, and he reigned over Israel for two years.
He did evil in the sight of the Lord and followed the ways of his father, the ways of his mother, and the ways of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who led Israel into sin.
He served Baal and worshiped him, provoking the Lord, the God of Israel, to anger, just as his father had done.
